channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Asia doubled down on future technology: South Korea named seven strategic growth engines from chips to fusion, Taiwan lined up a semiconductor investor summit, and China's humanoid-robot maker Unitree drew a CNY 61 billion IPO valuation.
item.description:
Across the region, governments and markets bet on the next technology wave. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said the country must ride its semiconductor strength into the "post-AI era" and named seven strategic growth engines — including small modular reactors (SMRs), nuclear fusion and advanced chips — with an ambition that stretches to a moon landing by 2030. In Taiwan, the stock exchange scheduled a themed SEMICON investor conference for 3 September, keeping the island's chip cluster in focus even as its firms navigate US restrictions. And in China, humanoid-robot maker Unitree launched its Shanghai IPO, offering about 40.45 million shares to raise roughly CNY 6.1 billion and reaching a valuation near CNY 61 billion, with close to 10 million investors subscribing — a milestone that symbolised both China's robotics ambitions and the froth in its IPO market. The common thread is a race to own the industries — chips, robotics, clean and advanced energy — expected to drive the next decade of manufacturing.

Industry Impact

This future-tech build-out is a long-run demand driver for specialty ACS materials. Semiconductors, robots, SMRs and advanced electronics all rely on high-performance adhesives, encapsulants, thermal-interface materials and protective coatings — higher-value, more technically demanding products than commodity construction lines. South Korea's growth-engine strategy and Taiwan's chip investment signal sustained capital flowing into exactly the segments where ACS suppliers can command a premium, and where qualification wins are sticky. The Unitree IPO underlines that China intends to scale humanoid and industrial robotics fast, expanding a manufacturing category that consumes bonding and coating materials. The strategic implication: continue building electronics- and robotics-grade product portfolios and technical-service capability in Asia's advanced-manufacturing hubs, since that is where the fastest-growing, highest-margin ACS demand is being created — even as commodity construction demand stays soft.

Lianhe Zaobao | Commercial Times | Wirtschaftswoche | Wirtschaftswoche

item.title: Brazil's presidential race opens this weekend, India said it stays in regular contact with Washington on a trade deal and floated a USD 10 billion transport-aircraft tender, and Argentina's country risk climbed ahead of its own vote.
item.description:
The emerging-market calendar filled up. In Brazil, the presidential campaign officially opens on 16 August with a candidate-registration deadline of 15 August and voting set for 4 October; incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is among the front-runners, making the direction of Latin America's largest economy a live question for the rest of the year. India kept working two tracks at once: Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said New Delhi and Washington remain in regular contact over a bilateral trade agreement even after the US slapped an additional 10% duty on Indian goods, while the defence ministry floated a roughly USD 10 billion (INR 1 lakh crore) tender for 60 medium transport aircraft to replace an ageing Soviet-era fleet — one of its biggest procurement drives in years. In Argentina, JP Morgan's country-risk gauge climbed more than 40 points in early August and hovered near the 400 mark as markets grew wary before the presidential election, while Pakistan offered a brighter note, reporting a primary budget surplus that beat its IMF target for a third straight year.

Industry Impact

Emerging markets are where much of the ACS industry's medium-term growth sits, so political and policy turning points there shape the demand map. Brazil's election will set the tone for construction, infrastructure and industrial policy in the largest Latin American market, where Mercosur trade dynamics also affect chemical flows — a reason to watch the 4 October outcome closely. India remains the standout structural growth story: continued US-trade engagement plus heavy defence and infrastructure spending underpin durable demand for industrial coatings, adhesives and sealants, even as the extra US tariff complicates its export math. Argentina's rising risk premium is a caution flag for exposure to a still-fragile economy. Net: keep India as a priority growth market for ACS investment, treat Brazil's demand outlook as election-contingent, and manage Argentine and other high-risk-premium markets conservatively.

China Economic Net | The Economic Times | The Hindu Business Line | The Times of India | La Nacion | The Express Tribune

item.title: China's factory engine stalled as July manufacturing activity slipped back into contraction, while expiring land-use rights on commercial buildings added a fresh threat to an already fragile property market.
item.description:
Two soft spots in China's economy came into focus. The official manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) — a gauge where readings below 50 signal contraction — fell back into contraction in July, which analysts attributed to a mix of seasonal effects, extreme weather and demand that had been pulled forward earlier in the year; July inflation data also drifted lower, pointing to weak underlying demand. The deeper structural worry is property. In China, land is leased rather than owned, and the land-use rights on a growing number of commercial buildings — shopping centres and offices — are now running down to less than 20 years, with no clear, uniform rule on renewal cost. That uncertainty is depressing valuations and investment in commercial real estate, layering a new problem onto the country's long housing slump. Local governments are responding with urban-renewal drives — cities such as Wuhan are courting investment to revive old factories and districts — but the property overhang remains a drag, and Hong Kong's market faces its own risk if Beijing extends a crackdown on offshore wealth.

Industry Impact

China is a huge market for construction chemicals, coatings and sealants, so renewed manufacturing contraction and a deepening commercial-property problem both point to soft near-term demand. Weak factory activity dampens industrial-coatings and adhesives volumes, while the land-use-rights overhang and stalled commercial construction hit exactly the building-materials and architectural-coatings segments ACS suppliers serve. The one offset is the government's urban-renewal push: retrofitting and renovating existing buildings — rather than new-build — favours repair, sealing and refurbishment products over volume construction adhesives, a mix shift ACS suppliers can position for. For companies exposed to China, the read is cautious: plan for subdued construction-linked demand, weight portfolios toward renovation and industrial-maintenance chemistries, and watch whether Beijing's stimulus and renewal programmes translate into real materials orders in the second half.

Commercial Times | Wallstreet:online | South China Morning Post | Hong Kong Commercial Daily

item.title: Only 23% of companies see real economic value from their AI investments, a WEF-KPMG study found, even as Washington encouraged firms to hack back at criminals and a hacking group claimed data stolen from about 50 major companies.
item.description:
A reality check landed on the AI boom. A study by the World Economic Forum and KPMG found only 23% of companies report economic value after deploying artificial intelligence, and just 6% see a significant impact; a separate Stanford analysis found a large share of the tasks workers actually want automated are not the ones AI is being pointed at. The gap between AI spending and measurable return is becoming the story. At the same time, the security side of AI is escalating: President Trump signed a national-security memorandum encouraging select US companies to launch their own cyberattacks against criminal hackers, working with the Justice and Homeland Security Departments — a significant shift toward private-sector "hack-back." The threat it responds to is real: a prolific hacking group claimed it stole large volumes of data from nearly 50 companies worldwide, including Philips, Shell and GE, and Taiwan said government agencies were hit last month by overseas AI-assisted cyberattacks. Industry groups are trying to bring rigour to adoption, with a new US supply-chain AI benchmark launched to track where the technology actually pays off.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers investing in AI across R&D, formulation, quality control and supply-chain planning, the WEF-KPMG finding is a useful corrective: most AI spending is not yet delivering measurable value, so the discipline is to target well-defined, high-return use cases — predictive maintenance, batch-quality analytics, demand forecasting — rather than broad rollouts. The security escalation is the more pressing operational risk. A wave of mass corporate breaches and state-linked, AI-assisted attacks raises the threat to chemical plants' operational-technology systems and to intellectual property such as proprietary formulations. The US "hack-back" memo also signals a more aggressive, less predictable cyber environment. Practical priorities: harden operational-technology and formulation-data security, treat suppliers' cyber posture as part of supply-chain risk, and hold AI projects to a clear value test before scaling.

La Nacion | The New York Times | BNN Bloomberg | Lianhe Zaobao | AP

item.title: The UK economy grew 0.4% in the second quarter, slowing from 0.6% but beating fears, while Poland expanded 3.8% and Thailand's growth is seen halving to about 1.7% — a picture of widening divergence across economies.
item.description:
Fresh output figures showed a two-speed world. The UK's Office for National Statistics reported that gross domestic product (GDP) rose 0.4% in the second quarter, cooling from 0.6% in the first, with a surprise 0.3% expansion in June driven by services; analysts called the economy more resilient than expected, and the reading is unlikely on its own to force the Bank of England's hand. Continental Europe's fast-growers kept powering ahead: Poland's economy expanded 3.8% year-on-year — roughly three times the EU average — shrugging off the energy shock from the Iran war. Elsewhere the momentum is fading: a Reuters poll of economists expects Thailand's growth to slow sharply from 2.8% to about 1.7% in the second quarter on weak household spending, and France reported only marginal improvement in the labour market for disabled workers, a reminder of persistent structural weakness. Taken together, the data show no single European or Asian trend — resilient services in the UK, strong catch-up growth in Central Europe, and softening demand in parts of Southeast Asia.

Industry Impact

Growth data set the demand backdrop for adhesives, coatings and sealants through their two biggest channels, construction and manufacturing. The UK's steady-but-slow 0.4% signals a flat market: not contracting, but offering little organic volume growth for building- and industrial-facing ACS lines. Poland's 3.8% is the more actionable number — Central and Eastern Europe remains the region where construction, appliance and automotive activity is expanding fastest, making it the priority growth market for ACS suppliers on the continent. Softer Thai growth, by contrast, tempers expectations for Southeast Asian demand this year. The overall divergence argues against treating "Europe" or "Asia" as single markets: ACS planners should tilt commercial resources toward the high-growth pockets (Poland and Central Europe) while managing mature Western European markets for share rather than volume, and keep Southeast Asian forecasts conservative.

The Guardian | Yahoo Taiwan | Les Echos | CNA | Les Echos

item.title: Global trade is proving more resilient than feared despite the Iran war and US tariffs: shipping giant Maersk raised its full-year outlook for the second time in seven weeks, citing strong Asian exports and firmer freight rates.
item.description:
Against a backdrop of war and tariff shocks, the plumbing of world trade is holding up. Container carrier A.P. Moller-Maersk raised its full-year guidance for the second time in seven weeks, crediting higher freight rates and a more resilient global economy than it had expected, and rival Hapag-Lloyd pointed to strong exports out of Asia and improved US demand. Maersk's chief executive Vincent Clerc said that even with the US–Iran conflict and additional US tariffs, demand and cargo volumes have kept climbing, though he cautioned that further disruption could still delay deliveries and push freight rates up. The resilience has a flip side visible elsewhere in the data: the "China plus one" relocation trend has slowed, with China's share of one big inspection firm's US-client sourcing steadying around 27% rather than continuing to fall — companies are finding it harder to leave China than the tariff rhetoric implies. For now, trade volumes are defying the pessimists even as the cost and risk of moving goods stay elevated.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers this is a genuinely encouraging counter-signal in an otherwise heavy news flow. Resilient container demand and rising freight volumes point to underlying manufacturing and consumption activity that is steadier than the war-and-tariffs headlines suggest — supportive for the industrial and packaging end-markets that consume adhesives, coatings and sealants. But the same story warns against complacency: firmer freight rates mean higher landed costs on imported feedstock and exported product, and Maersk's caution about renewed disruption keeps logistics risk elevated. The slowing "China plus one" shift also tells ACS strategists that wholesale supply-chain relocation is proving slow and costly, so plans premised on rapidly exiting China should be stress-tested. Net: read the trade resilience as modest demand support, but keep freight-cost inflation and re-routing risk in pricing and inventory planning.

Financial Post | Commercial Times | Commercial Times

item.title: Chinese carmakers could lift their share of Europe's market from about 10% now to as much as 30% by 2035, Citi analysts said, as new-energy vehicles topped half of China's car exports for a second straight month.
item.description:
Analysts put a number on how far Chinese cars could penetrate Europe. Citi's team, led by Harald Hendrikse, projects the market share of Chinese carmakers in Europe rising from around 10% in 2026 to between 15% and 30% by 2035, with the outcome hinging on how far the EU goes in tightening tariffs and imposing "made-in-EU" local-content rules. The export engine behind that ambition is shifting decisively electric: China's new-energy vehicles (NEVs) — battery-electric and plug-in hybrids — made up more than half of the country's car exports for a second consecutive month in July, and the domestic market saw 116 new or revamped models launched in the first half of the year, over three-quarters of them from homegrown brands. Beijing is also framing the export push as a virtue: an article in the Communist Party's People's Daily argued the global green transition needs China's "positive supply" and criticised "overcapacity"-based trade barriers — a direct rebuttal to European and US moves to shield their industries.

Industry Impact

Automotive coatings, adhesives and sealants are a major ACS revenue stream, so a structural shift in who builds Europe's cars matters directly. If Chinese brands take 15–30% of the European market, ACS suppliers face a choice between following those OEMs — many of which rely on established Chinese materials partners — or defending share with the incumbent European makers whose volumes would erode. The "made-in-EU" content rules Citi flags could be decisive: if the EU forces local production, Chinese carmakers will build plants in Europe, opening a window for European ACS suppliers to win qualification on those new lines. The electric mix compounds the shift, since EV bodies, batteries and electronics use a different, often adhesive-heavy bonding and thermal-management set than combustion cars. Strategic read: engage early with Chinese OEMs' European plant plans, and build EV-specific bonding and coating capability to capture the changing content per vehicle.

South China Morning Post | China Economic Net | Bjd.com.cn | Commercial Times

item.title: Japan's government shifted to back a near-term Bank of Japan rate hike, while benign US inflation data pushed traders to price out a September Fed increase, sending the S&P 500 to a record and leaving the two big economies on opposite tracks.
item.description:
The world's monetary cycles pulled further apart. In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government is now reported to support a Bank of Japan (BOJ) interest-rate hike as soon as September or October — a notable turn for an administration elected on loose fiscal policy — because a weak yen is pushing up import prices; the US, Japan and South Korea have also acted jointly to shore up the battered currency, and Japanese bond yields sit near record highs as traders bet on faster tightening. In the US the move is the other way. July consumer prices rose 3.4% year-on-year, in line with forecasts, and tame producer-price data followed, so traders cut their bets on a September Federal Reserve hike; the S&P 500 closed at a record. Fed officials are openly split — Richmond's Tom Barkin called a hike "an open question" while Cleveland's Beth Hammack pressed for an immediate increase to curb inflation. The net picture: the US is paused near the top of its cycle while Japan is only now tightening, keeping currencies and bond markets choppy.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers, interest rates feed through to construction and manufacturing — the two biggest end-markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants — and to the exchange rates that set feedstock costs and export competitiveness. A US inflation print that keeps the Fed on hold rather than hiking is mildly supportive: it steadies the financing costs behind construction pipelines and industrial capex into year-end. But the sharper signal is divergence. With the US paused and Japan tightening, the yen, dollar and other currencies will keep swinging, changing the relative cost of naphtha and specialty inputs and the competitiveness of exports region by region. A firmer yen would raise costs for Japanese chemical exporters while easing imported-input bills at home. ACS planners should assume flat-to-soft demand rather than a synchronized upturn, and build currency volatility into sourcing and pricing decisions.

Cnyes | Commercial Times | MarketScreener | MarketScreener | The Economic Times | The Standard

item.title: Detroit's carmakers warned that Washington's plan to rewrite the USMCA trade pact could add more than USD 2 billion a year to each company's costs, as Canada raced to avert a 50% tariff and Mexico asked the US to cut auto and steel duties.
item.description:
North America's trade machinery came under fresh strain. The three big Detroit automakers are preparing to warn the Trump administration that its proposed overhaul of the USMCA — the trade pact linking the US, Mexico and Canada — could cost each carmaker at least USD 2 billion a year and erode their edge against foreign rivals. The flashpoint is a US demand that vehicles contain at least 50% US-made content to qualify for tariff-free treatment, upending the integrated cross-border supply chains the industry was built on. The pressure is immediate: the US is set to impose new 50% tariffs on about CAD 20 billion of Canadian goods from 19 August, and Canada's negotiators met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on 13 August in a scramble to reach a deal before the deadline. Mexico, meanwhile, formally asked Washington to reduce or scrap tariffs on cars and steel during the USMCA review. Early damage is visible: US auto exports into Canada have fallen 13% since the trade war began, with South Korea filling part of the gap.

Industry Impact

Automotive is one of the largest end-markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants, so a forced reshaping of North American car production flows straight through to ACS demand. A 50%-US-content rule would pull assembly and parts work toward the US and away from Canadian and Mexican plants, redrawing where body-in-white adhesives, primers, coatings and sealing compounds are consumed. In the short term the uncertainty freezes investment decisions across the supply base — carmakers cannot commit to plant footprints while the rules are in flux — which tends to soften new-model tooling and materials orders. For ACS suppliers the read is to track content-rule outcomes plant by plant, keep flexible supply arrangements across all three USMCA countries, and watch the 19 August Canada tariff as the near-term trigger that could either de-escalate or harden into a broader North American trade rupture.

Handelsblatt | MarketScreener | El Financiero | The Globe and Mail | The Globe and Mail | POLITICO

item.title: A White House report accused more than 40 economies — including the EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Mexico and Canada — of helping China evade US tariffs through transshipment, and said AI tools will now be used to police the trade.
item.description:
The Trump administration escalated its tariff enforcement from rates to routes. A report titled "The Great Transshipment Scam," released by the White House Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy, accused more than 40 economies of forming a "shadow transshipment network" that lets Chinese goods reach the US relabelled through third countries to dodge tariffs. Trade adviser Peter Navarro singled out land neighbours Mexico and Canada alongside the EU, India, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan as the biggest enablers. To enforce it, the administration is building an AI-powered "detective border" that scans trade data to flag partners suspected of laundering Chinese exports. The pressure comes as the "China plus one" shift — companies moving sourcing out of China — is actually slowing: inspection firm QIMA found China's share of its US clients' procurement stopped falling and steadied around 27% in the second quarter. Separately, a planned US-China investment board meant to be a centrepiece of the coming Xi–Trump summit has stalled, with neither side having started talks.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers with globally spread supply chains, this raises compliance and routing risk across the board. If Washington treats transshipment as fraud and uses AI to trace component and material origins, companies will face tougher documentation demands on where inputs — resins, additives, packaging, electronics parts — actually come from, not just where the final product ships from. Being named puts the EU, Mexico, Canada and major Asian hubs under scrutiny precisely where much ACS-linked manufacturing sits. The slowing "China plus one" trend is a double message: relocating out of China is harder and slower than hoped, yet staying exposes suppliers to exactly this evasion crackdown. Practical steps: tighten country-of-origin traceability, review any China-linked intermediate inputs, and expect customs friction and audit risk to rise on cross-border chemical and packaging flows into the US.

Fortune | The Economic Times | Chinatimes | El Financiero | Commercial Times | Commercial Times

item.title: Regulation is redrawing the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) chain: 93% of US chemical makers say faster safety reviews would spur reshoring, while China's new environmental code and EU recycling rules push toward circular sourcing.
item.description:
The rulebook, not the oil price, drove the chemicals story today. In the US, a survey by the Society of Chemical Manufacturers & Affiliates (SOCMA) found almost 93% of manufacturers say a faster, more predictable review of new chemicals under Section 5 of the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) — the federal law that clears new substances before they can be sold — would make them more likely to reshore products and production to the US. In China, a new Ecological and Environmental Code takes effect on 15 August, shifting environmental rules from end-of-pipe clean-up toward a circular-economy model that rewards recycling and reuse across industry. In the EU, the industry body Plastics Europe pressed for the Waste Shipment Regulation to be made workable for intra-EU shipments of recyclable plastics, while France's Anti-Waste for a Circular Economy (AGEC) law is tightening producers' recycling and eco-design obligations. On the demand side, Taiwan's Changxing said it will invest TWD 1 billion to double capacity for organosilicon microspheres used in high-end copper-clad laminates — a reminder that specialty-materials demand from electronics is still expanding.

Industry Impact

This is Henkel's core environment, and because the drivers are regulatory they are durable rather than cyclical. Three forces are converging on ACS suppliers at once: a US push that ties faster chemical approvals to reshoring, so companies with US registration capacity and formulation agility gain first-mover advantage; a Chinese code that hard-wires circular-economy expectations into how products are made and disposed of; and EU recycling rules that reward recyclable, mono-material and reformulated chemistries. Together they raise the premium on compliant, sustainable adhesives, coatings and sealants and on the ability to move a formulation through different regulatory regimes quickly. The Changxing capacity expansion shows where the growth pockets sit — electronics-grade materials. Net: treat regulatory agility and circular-ready product lines as a commercial edge, not a compliance cost, and track the US TSCA reform closely as a potential reshoring trigger for North American demand.

SOCMA | China Economic Net | Plastics Europe | Challenges | Commercial Times | MAVESZ

item.title: Trump imposed tariffs of up to 100% on imported drones and their parts and moved to bar many foreign-made connected robots, prompting Germany's VDMA engineering association to warn the curbs isolate rather than protect industry.
item.description:
Washington opened a fresh, technology-focused tariff front. On 13 August President Trump signed a proclamation putting an ad valorem tariff of between 10% and 100% on imported drones and their components, citing national security; the full 100% rate hits larger or safety-sensitive drones and their docking stations, while smaller models face lower rates. In parallel, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has blocked the import and sale of a range of foreign-made connected robotic devices — from robot vacuums to pool cleaners — over data-collection and cybersecurity concerns, and the administration is drafting a broader rule to restrict connected robots that can map homes and capture Wi-Fi data. The measures land squarely on China, which now makes most of the world's consumer and industrial robots. Germany's VDMA — the mechanical-engineering association that speaks for much of Europe's machinery sector — pushed back hard: managing director Thilo Brodtmann called the robot import ban a policy of "isolation rather than cooperation" that will hurt industry on both sides. The move fits a widening pattern of US action against Chinese-linked hardware in drones, robotics and power electronics.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers, this is less about a single tariff line than about where the manufacturing base for their customers sits. Drones and robots are assembly-intensive products that use adhesives, protective coatings and sealants, so duties that reshuffle where they are built will, over time, move that demand between regions. More important is the direction of travel: the US is steadily walling off Chinese-linked industrial hardware, which pushes reshoring and "friend-shoring" of manufacturing — a tailwind for ACS suppliers with a footprint in the US and allied markets, and a headwind for those tied to Chinese export supply chains. VDMA's warning also signals friction for European machinery exporters caught between the two blocs. The practical takeaway: expect continued fragmentation of advanced-manufacturing supply chains, and position ACS capacity and technical support close to where robot, drone and electronics assembly is being pulled by policy.

Handelsblatt | Lianhe Zaobao | China Economic Net | VDMA | Dünya Gazetesi | Yahoo Taiwan

item.title: The Pentagon said it can hold its blockade of Iran's ports indefinitely as Iran's economy slides toward collapse, the IEA cut its 2026 oil-supply outlook by 4.3 million barrels a day, and Western oil majors booked record wartime profits.
item.description:
The war settled into a long, costly stalemate. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military has enough assets to keep the naval blockade of Iran going indefinitely; the US Navy has already turned back more than 55 commercial ships trying to run it and has boarded or disabled several. On the other side, Iran is buckling: a falling currency, runaway inflation, power cuts and job losses are spreading as the blockade chokes off the oil exports that fund the state, with analysts at Capital Economics noting oil sales abroad were the backbone of its economy. The market is re-pricing the disruption as durable rather than temporary. In its August report the International Energy Agency (IEA) — the rich countries' energy watchdog — said global oil supply will fall by about 4.3 million barrels a day this year to roughly 102 million, and Saudi Aramco's chief estimated the world has lost 2.6 billion barrels since the war began, with the daily gap now near 5 million barrels. Meanwhile the eight largest Western oil companies earned more than USD 700,000 of profit a minute over the spring quarter, and closed Middle East airspace kept throwing global air travel into disarray.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry, oil is the single biggest swing factor for input costs, and today's signals all point one way: structurally higher and more volatile prices for crude, naphtha and solvents deep into 2026 and beyond. When the Pentagon frames the blockade as open-ended and the IEA widens its supply cut, the planning base case shifts from "spike that reverses" to "sustained premium." The windfall profits at the oil majors are the mirror image of the cost pressure landing on chemical buyers downstream. Practical read for ACS producers: hold multi-quarter feedstock hedges and buffers rather than waiting for a reopening, treat single-day price dips as noise, and expect higher freight and insurance to keep compounding the raw-material bill. A weakening Iranian economy also raises the risk of sudden escalation, so scenario planning should keep an oil-shock case live.

The Economic Times | Les Echos | MarketScreener | Kompas | The Express Tribune | MarketScreener
